en: The Recorded Sayings of Great Master Miaoxu of Mount Touzi in Shuzhou, Compiled by his Dharma-heir Disciple Dao Kai, Resident of Mount Fuyong.

Ascending the hall to instruct the assembly, he said: "In the state of absolute correctness, there is no 'roundness. Within that roundness, there is still pervasiveness. In the state of total pervasiveness, there is no form."
Within form, the perfect circle remains; deeper still, it stirs the breath of dawn. As the sun sets, the heavens break into clear light.

In the place where the two courtyards blend in harmony, what is prized is the attainment of the profound mystery. When you, all of you, arrive here, how will you establish yourselves and find your livelihood?

How will you attain such resonance? After a long silence, he said: "The Master outside the curtain of night-clarity—throughout antiquity and today, no one has known him. One must surely look to the side..."
[The Master] raised his hand. "To plant a branch of the School of the Tree [of Enlightenment], these four lines of mine—how will you all, venerable practitioners of Chan, deliberate upon them?

At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "I have heard the Master’s words: 'Within the Perfect there is still pervasiveness; within form, however, the Perfect remains. What is the principle of this?
The Master said, "In the Right [the Center], the Mysterious is not established; in the Partial, one does not cling to things. The monk said, "It may indeed be called..."
"In darkness there is light; in light there is darkness. The Master asked, "Tell me, what principle is this? The monk said, "We are jointly trying to avoid the taboo.

The Master said, "One must understand it in this way. The monk then prostrated. The Master said, "The spring washes the moon before the railing; the sky stretches across the mountains beyond the rain.
Last night at Shaoshi, the Buddhas and Patriarchs slept soundly—how difficult, how difficult! He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he addressed his disciples, saying: "The wondrous Way penetrates the mind, transcending words and language; the profound path warms the body, leaving no trace of defilement.
How could the dragon’s nest or the phoenix’s offspring be of ordinary stock? Once this single mechanism is fully realized, who can discuss it?
O Zen masters, tell me: is this not the very form that fills the eyes and ears? At this very moment, do you know where it falls? The clouds and peaks are lofty..."
Rising above the peaks of the green mountains, where all phenomena are stilled to the east of the lofty crags; heaven and earth share the same spring. Who welcomes these scenes to the riverbank?
[The Master] strikes his staff once and says: "Even if one reaches ten parts of perfection, it is still but half the presentation.
At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked: "What is the occasion of the full presentation? The Master replied: "Śākyamuni Buddha."
[The Master] established the illusory city. A monk asked, "When you speak of provisional transformation and news, for whom do you say it?
The Master said, "The treasure site is near; take one more step. The monk said, "I am already at the place of treasure; how could I go further? The Master said, "One must indeed go in this manner."
The monk asked, "What kind of livelihood do you practice when you go out from another's house? The Master said, "Though I have no livelihood, it is far superior to wealth and nobility.
The monk asked, "What is your livelihood in the secret place? The Master said, "Majestic beyond the kalpas; nothing can disturb the Master."
The monk said, "Your countenance is most wonderful. He then prostrated. The Master said, "The laughter on Vulture Peak is flourishing; its fragrance and color are aromatic.
Amidst the assembly of the sages, there is no room for deliberation. Thereupon, he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he addressed his disciples, saying: "When one place is wondrous, ten thousand places are empty; when the three periods are understood, a thousand ages are the same.
In this profound stillness and vast silence lies the matter after realization; in this rushing and mournful sound lie the wind and the pines. Herein no one can apply rational principles;

therein no one possesses a deep insight into the midst of difference. When the essence functions as the utility, there is no distinction between them; this single piece of living mind has been attained."
Miaotong held up his staff and said, "Look, look! This is one who is hidden within the field;
this is a fellow who sports with supernatural powers. You must see him to truly see him. Among you, which monk is capable of seeing him?
Try to give old monk some breath of life! When you do, I shall bear witness for you. At that time, a monk stepped forward.
The assembly asked, "What is the wondrous principle of the source of the Great Way? The Master said, "A single moon universally contains all waters;
all moon-reflections in the waters are subsumed within that one moon. A monk asked, "In this way, are they the same or different?

The Master said, "Do you not see the meaning of the six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*? The monk asked, "What are totality, particularity, sameness, difference, formation, and disintegration?"
The Master drew a circle and said, "Within this single circle there is a Buddha. The monk asked, "What is this Buddha? The Master said, "His name cannot be avoided.
The monk then prostrated himself. The Master asked, "Why do you prostrate? The Master then said: "Within the same there is difference; within difference there is sameness.
The general and the particular merge to form a single tree of wind. The world is cool beneath its shade, and all people are therein. What need is there for further ripening?"
"Seeking the True Doctrine within the realms," he said, and then descended from his seat.
Upon entering the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Before the kalpas, the single breath is secretly and perfectly manifest.

Which of these is the one seal? It stands majestically, fully recorded. Sometimes, on the crystal palace, the jade maidens turn their heads; sometimes, before the ancient mirror stand, the stone man [stands still]."
Clapping his hands, [the Master] said: "Is there anyone who can recognize him? If you can identify him, I grant you this place of peace and bliss.
Here alone, with the flavor of the Dharma—equal and without distinction—you shall surely know the wondrous text of the falling nectar.
Today, this assembly of cloud-dwelling guests has come to my gate, treading through worn-out straw sandals; where do they intend to go? A single phrase, and all is clear."
"Transcending ten billion—what is this one phrase? Try and say it! Having spoken thus, he sat solemnly.
At that time, a monk came forward from the assembly and asked, "I, a student, do not understand; I pray the Master will expound upon it. The Master sat in silence.
The monk said, "I have heard that Vimalakīrti has an 'entrance into non-duality'—is this it? The Master laughed heartily and said, "This is mere inverted speech and perverse words."
The monk simply gave a slight smile and withdrew. The Master said, "I, the old monk, am at fault. The monk then prostrated. The Master said, "Go drink tea.
The monk said, "Master, you must be a 'white-handed thief' (a pickpocket). The Master said, "What have I stolen from you?
The monk said, "There is a mounting platform before the steps. The Master then ceased speaking. The Master then remarked, "If one speaks of the profound mystery or the single principle..."
It is appropriate. Some say that the ultimate destination of the three vehicles is clearly revealed; together they constitute the eight or nine stages of completion.

Today, Touzi has explained this for all you practitioners of Chan. Tell me, is this ordinary or is it sacred? Deliberate upon this: clouds embrace the blue peaks, waters wind through the cold forests.
If one does not do so, who can refine the gold? Thereupon, he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he addressed his disciples, saying: "The fire-gas is coldly radiant; the snow-mind is matured. When the Yang-Buddha comes and goes, the Yin-Demon appears and disappears.
Ultimately, what is it? On Mount Tiantai one sleeps on South Peak;
atop the summit of Shaoshi, one sits on Bear’s Ear. Looking left and right, he said: 'Keep your eyes wide open! Cease the field of right and wrong; sweep away likes and dislikes.'"
The family style is wondrous. From this point on, there is no further use for idle or empty phrases; not even a single thread hangs from the nine apertures. Venerable ones, tell me:
how does one who has attained it in a lifetime differ [from others]? At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "Master, have you attained it or not?
The Master said, "The eyebrows are above the eyelashes. The monk asked, "Where are the nostrils?"
The Master said, "You are not blind. The monk gave a great laugh. The Master said, "How can you deceive yourself?

The monk then departed. The Master then said, "If you can realize it upon the tip of the whisk and extract it from the tip of the staff—if you can do so, half-opening is acceptable and half-closing is also acceptable;
whether it is thus or not thus, both are acceptable. He then suddenly threw down the staff.
He said, "It is still that," and then descended from his seat.
On entering the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The sound of the knock enters the ear, yet the wind has no intent; the plum shadow lies across the window, yet the moon leaves no trace."
"What is it that is illuminated by this single wheel? Look and see—everyone is merely playing with their own vital spirit.

In the end, where does it all return? As for the place where it lands, look quickly with your eyes! If you can, in a single day, shift the pivot, you will surely become a man of the Way who has nothing to do.
If not, Old Yama will not permit you to remain. Do you understand? At that time, a monk stepped forth from the assembly.
Question: "What is a man of the Way who has nothing to do? The Master said: "When he wishes to walk, he walks;
when he wishes to sit, he sits. "How about you, monk? The monk said: "My conduct is clear and distinct; nothing obstructs me. The Master said: "What thing are you?"
The monk said, "How distressing! How distressing! The Master then struck him and said: "Silent and still, vast and remote;
wondrous and profound—what kind of functional application is this? Clear and pure, dark and obscure; silent and majestic—what sort of strategy is this? Try to say something!
All day long sitting peacefully in one hall, throughout the night in solitude beyond all discussion."—Qin Guang Zhengmai.
After transmitting the lineage, he smiled before the pivot of the mechanism, illuminating a unique fragrance. He then descended from his seat.
On ascending the hall, he addressed his disciples, saying: "Last night the wooden man slept in the chamber; this morning the stone woman leans against the solitary pine."
"What is the patriarch’s coming mechanism? Beneath one's feet, golden brilliance surpasses the jade phoenix; every single movement is vividly clear, the secret path is majestic and grand.
It fills and radiates everywhere, distinct day and night. A single light from the divine pearl draws forth the horizontal bone from within the darkness;
the winding path of the ant’s thread sits upon the tongue amidst the clarity. This is the place where monks tread. Great Virtues, how do you understand it?"

[The Master] looked on. At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and said, "The night is deep and there is no moonlight; what is 'the wooden man sleeping in his chamber'? The Master said, "Deep.
The monk said, "Daybreak has come and there is no sunlight; what is 'the stone woman leaning against a solitary pine'? The Master said, "Shallow."
The monk said, "When a single mechanism is clearly understood, what is the meaning of the Patriarch? The Master said, "Movement.
The monk said, "In the place where ten thousand miles are inexhaustible, what is the Golden Phoenix? The Master said, "Stillness. The monk prostrated and asked, "Ultimately, how is it?
The Master said, "Inwardly and outwardly void and mysterious; fundamentally empty and still. The monk then departed. The Master then said, "A single dharma."
It encompasses many dharmas. One Buddha seals all Buddhas; one mind unites a thousand minds; a single thought transcends ten thousand thoughts. Have you not seen the Way?
"When the sandalwood is brought and planted as a single tree, the color of its leaves is the same in spring wind and autumn.
Touzi speaks of the meaning in this way, and you all listen to the Dharma in this way; ultimately, there are no two distinct characteristics. Those with eyes will see for themselves. Thus it is said:

Descending from his seat, he ascended the hall and addressed his disciples, saying: "The mind and the Buddha have no fixed abode; they dwell in the station of awakening. They emit light and rain down flowers, moving the humans and devas.
Neither real nor unreal, this sublime Brahma-voice is fully endowed with ten thousand wonders. Do you see it? It stands solitary before you."
That which is luminously clear and has never possessed form or shadow is the Dharma of your own single mind. Thus, an ancient worthy said:
"In the kingdom of Silla, there was a son of the Buddha who, upon entering samādhi, was followed by the ten directions. This is precisely that.
Now tell me, you virtuous practitioners of Chan: when you ultimately enter samādhi, with what appearance do you perceive it? Is there even a portion of speech to answer this?
At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked: "To enter samādhi without moving body or mind—how is this principle?"
The Master said, "It is simply that which belongs to every person. The monk asked, "If that is so, why is it that one must enter samādhi?
The Master asked, "Tell me, what is 'entering deeply into samādhi'? The monk replied, "As for the sitting mat, it is certainly not lacking; I have simply never used it for prostrations.
The Master said, "So it is, so it is. The monk then performed a prostration. The Master then said, "Wondrous realization reaches its ultimate point; you must simply be one."
Whether manifesting the staff or the shout, whether discussing the Way or talking of Chan, there has never been a dharma distinct from the source itself.
This very nature is neither identical to nor separate from it. What thing is this? If you truly hit the mark, how would you differ from the Buddhas?
You descendants of my school must not let your hands be wounded by the blade; turn it over in your minds with a single breath and participate in the subtle purport together.
This is an excellent method. He then descended from his seat.
Upon ascending the hall, he instructed his disciples, saying: "The Dharma-gate of the ambrosia of liberation is wide open; penetrate into the heart-source adorned by the Avataṃsaka.
How wondrous it is to manifest spiritual powers through the samādhi of playful sport! How urgent it is to emerge within the sublime realm!"

Thus one accomplishes the Holy Path. When members of the monastic community have shed all traces of light and shadow and penetrated through to the very belly, at this very moment of total perfection—does there exist anyone who truly understands? Come forth and discuss it with this old monk!
At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "What is the Gate of Ambrosia? The Master said, "Look, look! Fortunately, there is a true consumer before the mountain."
[The monk] paused. The monk said, "Master, why do you leak [the truth] like this? The Master said, "I am bending over backward for your sakes.
The monk said, "Is this not turning the unsurpassed Dharma-wheel? The Master said, "What are you saying? The monk then gave a shout. The Master struck him.

The monk said, "This kindness is difficult to repay. The Master said, "This resentment is difficult to requite. The Master then said, "The ground of returning to one's seat is subtle and profound, difficult to reach."

The practice of the patch-robed monks is vast and remote, yet intimate by nature. The Tathāgata’s sudden teaching and the patriarchs’ mind-to-mind transmission—every mountain peak, high or low, is a matter of entrustment.
Do you see it? Raising his whisk, he called out in a loud voice, "Venerable ones! What is this?
He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he addressed his disciples, saying: "The sea gates are quiet in autumn; the cries of geese are rare. The river waters are limpid, reflecting myriad subtle forms.
What a fine golden hue adorns the human world! Yellow maples, leaf by leaf, fly forth all at once.
This state is clear and distinct, majestic and manifest everywhere. Even so, truly there are few who understand. Do you all, venerable practitioners, understand?

Ruler and minister, pervasiveness and correctness, all together are not employed. Essence and function, guest and host—all are merely arrangements. To say they are simply ordinary is itself a great difficulty.

If one were to secretly apply ornamental weapons, there would be no need for a single character; yet if one were to suddenly attempt to search for them, the meaning of the "Three Emptinesses" would not yet be seen.
Touzi’s report in this manner is already like adding jade to the snow or adding mud to the earth. How [could it be otherwise]?
"It is thus. Pure jade has no flaws; carved patterns destroy its virtue. What do you think, Great Assembly?
At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "If it is self-knowing, why do you not doubt it? The Master struck him, saying, "Who can escape this nest?"
The monk said, "Preceptor, do not deceive me by striking me. The Master threw down his staff and asked, "What will you do now?
The monk laughed loudly, "He-he! and went out. The Master called out, "Come here, *śrāmaṇera*! The monk paid him no heed.
The Master said, "A lion, with a single drop of milk, scatters sixteen *hu* of donkey's milk. The Master then continued, "I have just now, for the sake of the assembly, leaked [the secret]."
There are not a few who linger here. But do you know where they have fallen? The "Four Sevens" of India did not know their place; the "Two Threes" of this land did not accept the time.
At the foot of the peak, the sound of a spring flows through a single ravine; atop the mountain, the misty trees have branches swaying in the wind.
All you practitioners of Zen: how, after all, are these four lines of mine to be understood? Long-standing seniors of the Way, look! Then he descended from his seat.
The Master then said to the assembly, "Touzi has three vessels. Today I shall present them to you; listen closely.
You must perform a marvelous melody with a sublime style. As for the 'Vessel of the Superior Correctness'—how do you all see it?
With a masterful hand, the strings are plucked to produce the Jade Tune. As for the 'Vessel of the Central Appropriateness'—how do you all see it? Truly..."
With living eyes, one sees through and breaks open the countenance of heaven. As for those of inferior capacity, how do you all see?
The assembly remained silent. The Master spoke again: "Those of superior rectitude may ascend further; those of middling aptitude may realize themselves."

"A person of inferior capacity may be acceptable for the present time. If, moreover, the three positions are all reached simultaneously, this is the 'person of no-position' (mujishi-jinin). Take care.
The Master then said to the assembly, "Today I recall the words of my former teacher regarding the phrase of 'ordinary and birthless' (hyōjō mushōku): 'Subtle, profound, and without..."
The phrase of no-self (wusi). The phrase of the essence being luminous and inexhaustible (ti-ming wujin ju). You all, each of you, deliberate upon these one by one. It is further said:
Only when you penetrate the phrase of non-arising (wusheng ju) do you attain the Dharma-body; only when you penetrate the phrase of no-self do you reach that other shore;
only when you penetrate the phrase of the inexhaustible do you attain what is before your eyes. When these three phrases are ultimately attained and each is fully understood—monks, take heed!
The Master then said to the assembly: "The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains six kinds of causal conditions: sometimes they are collective, sometimes individual;

sometimes identical, sometimes distinct; sometimes forming, and sometimes disintegrating. O virtuous practitioners of meditation, how ultimately do you comprehend these? These six characteristics are in fact but a single characteristic:
collectively they are the Buddha, individually they are the mind, identical they are the Dharma, distinct they are thought, forming they are the Sangha, and disintegrating they are deluded emotion."
"Sealed by the single Buddha throughout all things.
Be careful. The Master then said to the assembly: "The Sūtra says: 'The triple world is but the one mind; outside the mind there are no separate dharmas.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Where does this meaning land its beak? [He picks up a pair of fire tongs and says: This..."
In this state, is there still mind, Buddha, or sentient beings? If there is none, why is it called "the one mind"?
How would you explain this? My late teacher said: "The triple world is but the one mind. Do you see me now? This principle is most rare;
try to speak of it. Take care.
The Master then said to the assembly: "The wondrous existence and wondrous function are not matters of meritorious achievement; how could they be reached by worldly principles?

Why is this so? Before the Tathāgata appeared in the world to turn the Wheel of Dharma in the Western Heaven, and before the Patriarchs came from the West to transmit the Mind-Seal to this land—tell me, what thing turns, and what thing is transmitted? As the mountain clouds drift slowly, the river waters flow on.
Tao. After a long silence, he said: "Wild chrysanthemums hold gold; the Han spring gurgles jade. Behold the distinctness of this news:
it has long been unattainable. Take care."
The Master then said to the assembly, "Seeing form is seeing the mind; hearing sound is awakening to the Way. Transcending form and transcending the mind, one sees form and clarifies the mind.
He then asked, "Tell me, with what do you deliberate? Holding up a round fan, he said, "This is seeing form and seeing the mind."
Touzi spoke thus to expose the truth. Since these are superfluous words, O Zen practitioners, can you say that they have been grasped?
He sets down his round fan and says: "Even so, what kind of mental activity is this? Adieu!
The Master thereupon said to the assembly: "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive.
This would startle the "Yellow-Faced Old Man" (the Buddha) to death and deceive the Great Śāriputra. Nevertheless, it is only by reaching this very ground that one attains it.
What principle is this? It is the ultimate true mark and true nature, manifesting as activity and movement—precious indeed.
[The Master] spoke again, saying to the assembly: "In the past, the Great Master Bodhidharma transmitted the mind-seal alone, revealing it to those on the path of delusion.

This was a separate transmission outside the teachings, not established through words and letters. Is there anyone here who knows where this falls? Who knows that there is still [a way] within the teachings?"
As for words, who can truly know the underlying principle? To speak of them is to express that which lies beyond the external. Furthermore, tell me: why did he say to me, "I do not recognize you"?
This mountain monk is far too reckless. Take care.
The Master then said to the assembly: "Chan does not reside in intellectual comprehension; how could the Way be sought through worldly sentiments?

It was only upon meeting Master Huiyuan that I came to know there is a Great Matter, which is not something to be trifled with or manipulated at will. Let the assembly try to bring forth the jewel within your hearts and present it for me to see. Take care."
The Master then said to the assembly, "Today I shall present to you the Five Ranks of my late teacher, Master Dongshan.
Examine each one thoroughly: the True within the Middle is the Pervasive; the False within the Middle is the Universal; the True within the False is the Universal and Middle;
the Perfect within the Perfect is Coming from the Middle; Form within Form is Reaching the Universal; and the Subtle within the Subtle is Arriving at the Convergence. Thus he finished.

Ultimately, there are five positions, yet each position is without a fixed position. The wondrous manifestation of emptiness reveals the Truth. What, after all, is this Truth? Be careful! There is a verse that says:
"Returning, it was originally the pervasiveness within the Middle; Advancing, the Middle is intimately within the pervasive.

If it does not come, it is difficult to discern its coming from the Middle; If it does not go, it is difficult to know its arrival at the Convergence. The pervasiveness and the Middle are distantly severed; one arrives through the Convergence."
"Clearly manifest before the Great Ultimate of the single breath. After the rain, the clouds disperse and the sky is as if washed clean.
How does the sound of the bell enter the ancient pines and the wind? He further said: "Do you all know? If you can capture it in a sketch and attain it, I grant that you possess it.
With one stroke of the dark tally that avoids birth and death, you will then know the place where the crack cannot be avoided. Now tell me, what was the meaning of the Old Man of Xinfeng?"
They only attend to the crying of the child, yet forget their own ugliness. Today, Touzi once again reveals his own clumsiness;
do not say it is good to others. Even though it is so, who is truly one who has attained the reality and reached the ultimate? Come forth and deliberate with me.
Be careful.
When the Master first arrived at the place of Chan Master Yuanjian, Yuanjian welcomed him and paid his respects. The Master remained silent.

Yuanjian then instructed him to contemplate the dialogue concerning the outsider who asked the Buddha whether he spoke of existence or non-existence. Having received these instructions, the Master sat in the hall for three years.
On one occasion, when Yuanjian asked him, "Do you still remember the critical phrase? the Master was about to analyze it when Yuanjian suddenly covered the Master's mouth.
The Master said, "You have understood it at the point where there was a long silence. At these words, the Teacher suddenly attained great enlightenment and prostrated himself.
Guanding asked, "Have you wondrously awakened to the profound mechanism? The Teacher replied, "Even if there were such a thing, I must spit it out.

At that time, Attendant Zhi, who was standing by, saw this and remarked, "Master Qing Huayan is like one who has recovered from an illness through the breaking of a sweat. The Teacher looked back and said: [The text ends here.]
He joined his mouth to the dog’s; if it barked again, I would vomit. From then on, another three years passed.
When the time was ripe, [Zhaozhou] emerged from the cave and presented the fundamental principles to him. [Guishan] found them all to be wondrously in accord and bestowed them upon him.

He then entrusted him with eighteen items—including the *dingxiang* (cranial image) of Master Dayang, leather sandals, and a lined robe—along with his wondrous realizations, saying: "In my stead, continue this ancestral style."

"Do not linger here for long; you must properly protect and uphold [the Dharma]. He then wrote a verse to send him, saying: "The Sumeru stands in the great void, The sun and moon revolve as its attendants.
As the myriad peaks gradually lean toward it, The white clouds are just beginning to change. A breeze rises from the small forest grove, At Caoxi, the curtains are rolled back.
The golden phoenix dwells in the dragon’s nest; How could the imperial moss be crushed by a carriage wheel? He then ordered Yi to rely upon Yuan Tongxiu.
At the Chan Master’s quarters, the Master arrived but did not inquire about anything; he did nothing but indulge in sleep.

An attendant reported this to Xiu, saying, "There is a monk in the hall who sleeps every day; the monastic regulations should be enforced. Xiu asked, "Who is it? The attendant replied, "The Senior Monk Qing."
Xiu said, "Not yet; wait until I have inspected it. Xiu then dragged his staff into the hall.
Seeing the Master fast asleep, he struck the head of the bed and scolded him, saying, "There is no leisure food here for you, Venerable Sir, to eat and then fall into a deep sleep.
The Master asked, "What am I to do, as instructed by the Abbot? Xiu said, "Why do you not go practice Zen? The Master replied, "Fine food does not..."

"Those in the middle get fat while the people eat [the leftovers]. Xiu said, "What can be done? There are many who refuse to take the seat. The Master said, "If they wait until they are willing, what would that be worth?
Xiu asked, "Whom have you, Venerable Seat-holder, encountered? The Master replied, "The Venerable Fuyan Yuan. Xiu said, "No wonder you are so stubborn and unruly.
They shook hands and laughed together, then returned to the abbot’s quarters. From this point on, his reputation for the Way spread widely.

One day, while the Master was sitting in his quarters, a monk named Dao Kai came to pose a question: "The words and phrases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are like the common tea and rice of daily life;
apart from these, do you have any other way of guiding people? The Master replied, "You say that within the cosmic realm..."
The Son of Heaven issued a decree. [Huangbo] asked, "Would you even borrow the examples of Yu, Tang, Yao, and Shun to serve as a model for your speech?
He then shook his whisk over Kai’s mouth and said, "From the moment you first conceived this intention, you already deserved thirty blows.
At these words, Kai attained great enlightenment. The Master asked, "What principle have you seen? Kai bowed and departed. The Master said, "You have reached the state beyond doubt."
"Is this not the ground [of realization]? Kai covered his ears and departed. The Master was greatly pleased and granted him permission.
One day, while seated, the Master called to his disciples, saying: "I have a single phrase. All you practitioners of Chan, offer your words. He then spoke on their behalf, saying:
"I do not refuse to speak it to you all, yet I fear it might bring trouble upon my descendants. Thereupon he uttered this verse: "Majestic and lofty..."

He assumed the dignified bearing of a king, manifesting the wondrous Way with majestic presence. "I have a single phrase," he said, "which would allow even a donkey to carry forth the entire ancestral wind.
He also said, "The same. One day, as the Master entered the hall, there was a monk who was sleeping. The Master remarked, "It is just like me when I was at Yuantong Chan Monastery."
The Master engaged in a dialogue similar to this. The monk remained silent. The Master said, "Have you captured it? As the monk was about to explain, the Master struck him.
At that moment, the monk attained a sudden, great awakening and prostrated himself. The Master asked, "What have you seen that you prostrate yourself?
The monk replied, "Today it is as if a poor man has obtained a bright pearl. The Master departed with a joyful expression. The monk went straight on.
He went up to the Abbot’s quarters to report the matter. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Go away for now.
Postscript to the *Recorded Sayings of the Great Master Miaoxu of Mount Touzi in Shuzhou*:
The Master’s name was Yiqing; by secular surname, he was a son of the Li clan of Qingzhe. At the age of seven, he displayed exceptional brilliance. He went of his own accord...

He left the household life at Miaoxiang Monastery. Having passed the scriptural examinations, he received ordination and studied the *Śataśāstra*. Before long, he remarked, "The path of the three great aeons is far and long; what benefit is there in exhausting oneself?
He then entered Luoyang to listen to the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, grasping it as clearly as if threading beads. His appreciation and protection [of the teachings] were uninterrupted.

Once, while reading the verses of the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, he reached the passage on the "intrinsic nature of the mind" and had a sudden realization, saying, "The Dharma is free from words and letters."

"How could I not preach? he thought, and immediately abandoned his solitary wandering to attend the patriarchal seat. At that time, the Chan Master Fushan Yuanjian, the Venerable Fayuan, was residing at Huisheng Rock.
One night, he dreamed of holding a blue hawk in his hand; this was considered an especially auspicious omen.
At dawn, the Master arrived. Huiyuan welcomed him with formal rites; the details of their karmic connection and the opening words of their dialogue may be seen in the preceding chapter.
The world calls him "Green Eagle"—is this perhaps who that refers to? Others also say he was "Green Huayan," likely because he took the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his primary field of study.
Furthermore, he was in accord with the Great Master Dayang An; he continued the lineage of the Dongxia school, yet did not raise [his own] banner.
The world was [ruled] for thirteen years. Dayang (Daiyang) transmitted the Dharma-gāthā to the Venerable Fayuan (Fayuan Heshang), saying:

"The grass on the peak of Mount Guang; leaning upon you, it awaits the refining fire. Where the extraordinary sprouts flourish most luxuriantly, there the profound and secret spiritual roots are firmly established. The end of that gāthā says:
One who has attained the Dharma remains hidden among the masses for ten years before finally responding to the call to propagate it. Master Faryuan received [the transmission] from him.
He offered his own praise of his teacher’s *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance), saying: "A black dog with hooves of refined silver; a white elephant ridden by the Kunlun.
Unimpeded in these two, a wooden horse neighs amidst the flames. Faryuan then bestowed such things as these upon the Master, and the Master accepted them all.
Thus, he engaged in various communal labors for twelve years. Thereafter, he sang the "Snow Song" of Xinfeng and arranged the wondrous "Lamp" of Dongshan.
For over a thousand generations, he served as a model for Buddhas; for three or four years, he manifested the functional pivot of the Patriarchs.
Solely continuing the lineage of Yang Guang, he raised the sword that refines and heats [the mind], and at the peak of Touzi Mountain, the dragon roared.
The dance of the golden phoenix; within the land of the Great Tang, the tiger reveals the hooves of the jade unicorn.

He has deeply entered the realm of the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) without deviation, and stably manifests the boundless, wondrous marks of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. Those who appeared as his Dharma heirs numbered eight.
Dao Kai resided at Furong; Yuan Yi resided at Shimen; Weizhao resided at Letan;
Facheng resided at Jingyin; Shousui resided at Dahong; Miaorong resided at Baishui; Liaqi resided at Ziyang;
and Chali resided at Yungai. These great masters formed branches and extended vines, like jade turning and pearls rolling.
[The text] concludes. The Master said, "The general outline is thus. How could it be attained through the clamor of words and phrases? He was posthumously granted the title of Great Master Miaoxu.
Written to completion by the śramaṇa Zichun, a third-generation descendant residing at Mount Danxia, who hurriedly took up his brush.
